name: Shidare Katsura of Ryugen-ji

location.address: Ryugen-ji temple, Ohgayu, Morioka City, Iwate Prefecture

access: Free, on temple grounds (behind the main hall, at the edge of the graveyard); Ryugen-ji is an ordinary working Soto Zen temple, grounds open, no gate or booking involved
transport: No station nearby; Ohgayu is a rural district outside central Morioka, reachable by car
verify_notes: A genuinely rare weeping-form variant of an ordinary katsura, which is why it and two clonal sister specimens elsewhere in Morioka (at 'Kado' and 'Sakanacho') were designated together as a single national Natural Monument (国指定天然記念物, simply named 'Shidarekatsura') on 9 December 1924 -- the designation covers three named individual trees, this one being at Ryugen-ji (瀧源寺, temple founded 1574, Soto Zen). History per the Morioka city board of education's own 1994 on-site sign (relayed on both ja.wikipedia and hitozato-kyoboku.com): the original weeping katsura was found wild in the mountains of Uchikawame, Ohasako (now part of Hanamaki), roughly 400 years ago, first transplanted to Myosen-ji temple, then moved again to Ryugen-ji by its founding priest. That original trunk grew to over 30m before being felled in 1824 (Bunsei 7) for timber to repair the main hall; the tree standing today grew from a sucker off the old stump, which is why its age (roughly 180 years per the 1994 signage, so by calculation nearer 200-215 years now in 2026) is much younger than the tree's own documented history. Height ~21m, girth (目通り幹囲, measured at breast height) ~3.5m/350cm per the same 1994 sign -- note this single physical measurement is what both Wikipedia and hitozato-kyoboku.com repeat, so treat it as one underlying data point cited twice rather than two separate measurements, though the tree's existence, species, location and designation are corroborated independently by the Commons photograph (Ty19080914, 4 May 2018, CC BY-SA 4.0, directly captioned 'Shidare Katsura of Takigenji'), which also confirms it was alive and in leaf in 2018. Exact coordinates (39.6134, 141.2366) come from hitozato-kyoboku.com's own stated lat/long, given to within a second of arc, matching a temple compound so treated as confirmed. A sister tree at 'Kado' in Morioka (22m, girth 3.3m, ~140 years, also 1924-designated) is shown in the second Commons photo for this candidate (File:Shidarekatsura_Kado.jpg) but I could not find its exact address within this pass's time budget -- flagging it in my report as a separate lead worth a short follow-up rather than pinning it speculatively here.
